title: Best Thermostat Settings for Sleep and Allergies
h1: What Are the Best Thermostat and HVAC Settings for Sleep and Allergies?
description: Most people sleep best in a cool room, around the mid-60s. Learn thermostat, fan and humidity settings that help with sleep and allergies in a San Diego home.
quick_answer: Most people sleep best in a cool bedroom, roughly 60 to 68 degrees, so set your thermostat a few degrees cooler at bedtime than during the day. For allergies, use a good pleated filter, run the fan on a circulate or auto setting rather than off, and keep indoor humidity in a moderate range, about 30 to 50 percent.
body:
What temperature is best for sleeping?

Your body temperature naturally drops as you fall asleep, and a cool room helps that happen. Sleep researchers generally point to a range in the 60s, with many people landing somewhere around 65 degrees. There's no perfect number for everyone, so treat that as a starting point and adjust a degree or two at a time.

A few things to keep in mind:

  • Thermostats are usually in a hallway, not your bedroom. The bedroom may run warmer or cooler than the reading, especially upstairs.
  • Bedding matters as much as the setting. A heavy comforter at 65 can feel like 72.
  • Babies and older adults may need a different setting. Follow your pediatrician's or doctor's advice.

How should you program the thermostat for night?

Set your sleep temperature to start about 30 minutes to an hour before bedtime, so the room is already cool when you lie down. Then let it warm back up about half an hour before you wake. That makes getting out of bed easier on winter mornings.

In San Diego's mild climate the setback doesn't need to be dramatic. Near the coast, many nights need little or no heating or cooling at all. Inland, winter nights can get cold enough that the heat runs, and summer nights after a hot day may need AC to pull the house down.

If you have a heat pump, avoid huge overnight setbacks in winter. A big jump in the morning can bring on backup electric heat, which costs more to run. A smaller setback, or a smart thermostat with adaptive recovery, handles that better.

What fan setting is best for allergies?

Your filter only cleans air that moves through it. On mild nights the system may barely run, so the filter sits idle while dust and dander settle in the bedroom.

  • Auto runs the fan only when heating or cooling. Fine for most nights when the system cycles regularly.
  • Circulate, if your thermostat has it, runs the fan part of every hour even when nothing else is running. This is often the best choice for allergy sufferers.
  • On runs the fan nonstop. It filters the most, but uses more electricity and in summer can re-evaporate moisture off the coil and raise humidity.

Pair the fan setting with a quality pleated filter. For most homes, something in the MERV 11 to 13 range is a good target if the system can handle it.

Does humidity affect sleep and allergies?

Yes. Dust mites and mold both like humid air. Very dry air, on the other hand, can leave your nose and throat irritated, which is common during Santa Ana wind events when the humidity drops sharply.

A moderate indoor range, roughly 30 to 50 percent, is a good target. Near the coast, a dehumidifier or simply running the AC can help on muggy nights. Inland during dry spells, a humidifier can make the bedroom more comfortable. An inexpensive hygrometer will tell you where you actually are.

What else helps you sleep better with allergies?

  1. Keep bedroom vents open and unblocked by furniture so the room gets its share of filtered air.
  2. Close windows on high-pollen days, during Santa Ana winds and when there's wildfire smoke in the area.
  3. Add a portable HEPA purifier in the bedroom for extra filtration where you spend a third of your day.
  4. Keep the system clean. A dirty coil or dusty ducts can put allergens right back into the air you're filtering.
  5. Quiet things down. If the system is noisy enough to wake you, that's worth a service call. Rattles and squeals usually mean something needs attention.

If one bedroom never gets comfortable no matter what you set, the problem is often ductwork or airflow rather than the thermostat. Our HVAC technicians can check airflow, add zoning, or install a smart thermostat set up for your schedule. For allergy-focused upgrades, see our indoor air quality services.
faqs: Is it bad to turn the AC off at night?

Not if the house stays comfortable. Near the coast many homes do fine with the system off overnight. Inland, a hot house may stay too warm to sleep well. If you turn it off, the filter isn't cleaning the air either, so consider a circulate fan setting or a bedroom purifier.
Should I sleep with the fan on or auto?

Auto is fine for most people. If you have allergies, a circulate setting is a good compromise because it moves air through the filter regularly without running the fan all night. Running it fully on can raise summer humidity and costs more in electricity.
Why is my bedroom warmer than the thermostat setting?

The thermostat only reads the temperature where it hangs. Bedrooms far from the air handler, over the garage or upstairs often run warmer because of duct length, leaks or poor insulation. A technician can check airflow to that room and suggest fixes like duct sealing, balancing or zoning.
Can a smart thermostat help with sleep?

It can make it easier. You can set a bedtime and wake schedule, adjust from bed with your phone, and some models use a remote sensor in the bedroom so they control the temperature where you actually sleep.
